text.p: Management board chairman Friedel Neuber of Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale said late on Wednesday that he expected "satisfactory" annual results for 1996, with profits holding around 1995 levels.

"We will hold 1996 profit levels at 1995 levels," Neuber told journalists at a seminar in Frankfurt, adding that he expected operating profits before risk provisions in the first nine months to the end of September 1996 to rise ten percent.

He said net profit was broadly in line with the good results of the previous year. In 1995, WestLB reported an operating profit, before risk provisions, of 1.829 billion marks ($1.21 billion), with net profits of 520 million marks.
The group's trading surplus in particular was higher than in the previous year, while net earnings grew slightly and net commissions received grew strongly in the nine-month period.
Neuber also said that the troubled German engineering firm Deutsche Babcock AG, in which WestLB has a 10 percent stake, faced drastic cuts as part of its restructuring programme.
Deutsche Babcock would have to sell off a number of its subsidiaries, and comprehensive changes in the personnel structure were needed, the WestLB chief said.
"The group will be slimmed down," Neuber said, declining to put a figure on any potential job losses, adding that he was convinced that the restructuring package would be a success.
Deutsche Babcock last week categorically denied rumours on the Frankfurt stock exchange that it was facing insolvency and said that its restructuring programme was going well.
Neuber was critical of the recent probe by German tax authorities probe into suspected tax-evasion at branches of WestLB and other savings banks.
"Banks can only point out to a customer what their tax requirements, not improve the customer's behaviour when it comes to fulfilling those requirements," Neuber said.

In early September, German tax authorities investigated the branches on suspicion that WestLB employees helped customers in evading taxes, with suspicions of illegal transfers of funds to Luxembourg and Switzerland.
Neuber said that the bank had told its employees in 1992 and 1993 that customers should be made aware that interest income from Luxembourg and Switzerland was also liable for German income tax.
Employees had been told that any consultation with the customer should be broken off, if a customer seemed not to be complying with the law, said Neuber.
Neuber said he hoped the investigation by the tax authorities would be concluded soon, so that WestLB could examine the results in detail.
